---
name: hunk-review
description: Interacts with live Hunk diff review sessions via CLI. Inspects review focus, navigates files, hunks, and exact lines, reloads session contents, adds inline review comments, and paints attention marks on character ranges. Use when the user has a Hunk session running or wants to review diffs interactively.
---

# Hunk Review

Hunk is an interactive terminal diff viewer. The TUI is for the user -- do NOT run `hunk diff`, `hunk show`, or other interactive commands directly. Use `hunk session *` CLI commands to inspect and control live sessions through the local daemon.

If no session exists, ask the user to launch Hunk in their terminal first.

## Workflow

```text
1. hunk session list                                    # find live sessions
2. hunk session get --repo .                            # inspect path / repo / source
3. hunk session review --repo . --json                  # inspect file/hunk structure first
4. hunk session review --repo . --include-patch --json  # opt into raw diff text only when needed
5. hunk session context --repo .                        # check current focus when needed
6. hunk session navigate ...                            # move to the right place
7. hunk session reload -- <command>                     # swap contents if needed
8. hunk session comment add ...                         # leave one review note
9. hunk session comment apply ...                       # apply many agent notes in one stdin batch
10. hunk session highlight add ...                      # light up the exact range you are explaining
```

## Session selection

Most session commands accept:

- `--repo <path>` -- match the live session by its current loaded repo root (most common)
- `<session-id>` -- match by exact ID (use when multiple sessions share a repo)
- If only one session exists, it auto-resolves

`reload` also supports:

- `--session-path <path>` -- match the live Hunk window by its current working directory
- `--source <path>` -- load the replacement `diff` / `show` command from a different directory

Use `--source` only for advanced reloads where the live session you want to control is not already associated with the checkout you want to load next. For a normal worktree session, prefer selecting it directly with `--repo /path/to/worktree`.

## Commands

### Inspect

```bash
hunk session list [--json]
hunk session get (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--json]
hunk session context (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--json]
hunk session review (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--include-patch] [--include-notes] [--json]
```

- `get` shows the session `Path`, `Repo`, and `Source`, which helps when choosing between `--repo` and `--session-path`
- `Repo` is what `--repo` matches; `Path` is what `--session-path` matches
- `review --json` returns file and hunk structure by default; add `--include-patch` only when a caller truly needs raw unified diff text
- `review --include-notes` also returns the live review notes alongside the file and hunk structure

### Navigate

```bash
hunk session navigate (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--hunk <n> | --old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) [--json]
hunk session navigate (<session-id> | --repo <path>) (--next-comment | --prev-comment) [--json]
```

Absolute navigation requires `--file` and exactly one of `--hunk`, `--new-line`, or `--old-line`:

```bash
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --hunk 2
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 372
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --old-line 355
```

Relative comment navigation jumps between annotated hunks and does not require `--file`:

```bash
hunk session navigate --repo . --next-comment
hunk session navigate --repo . --prev-comment
```

- `--hunk <n>` is 1-based
- `--new-line` / `--old-line` are 1-based line numbers on that diff side
- A line target lands the user's viewport on that exact line (falling back to its hunk when the line is inside a collapsed region); `--hunk` lands on the hunk
- Use either `--next-comment` or `--prev-comment`, not both

### Reload

Swaps the live session's contents. Pass a Hunk review command after `--`:

```bash
hunk session reload (<session-id> | --repo <path> | --session-path <path>) [--source <path>] [--json] -- diff [ref] [-- <pathspec...>]
hunk session reload (<session-id> | --repo <path> | --session-path <path>) [--source <path>] [--json] -- show [ref] [-- <pathspec...>]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff main...feature -- src/ui
hunk session reload --repo . -- show HEAD~1
hunk session reload --repo . -- show HEAD~1 -- README.md
hunk session reload --repo /path/to/worktree -- diff
hunk session reload --session-path /path/to/live-window --source /path/to/other-checkout -- diff
```

- Always include `--` before the nested Hunk command
- `--repo` or `<session-id>` usually selects the session you want
- `--source` is advanced: it does not select the session; it only changes where the replacement review command runs
- If the live session is already showing the target worktree, prefer `hunk session reload --repo /path/to/worktree -- diff`
- `--session-path` targets the live window when you need to keep session selection separate from reload source

### Comments

```bash
hunk session comment add (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) --summary <text> [--rationale <text>] [--author <name>] [--markup <stml>] [--focus] [--json]
hunk session comment apply (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --stdin [--focus] [--json]
hunk session comment list (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--type <live|all|ai|agent|user>] [--json]
hunk session comment rm (<session-id> | --repo <path>) <comment-id> [--json]
hunk session comment clear (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--include-user|--all] --yes [--json]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session comment add --repo . --file README.md --new-line 103 --summary "Tighten this wording"
printf '%s\n' '{"comments":[{"filePath":"README.md","newLine":103,"summary":"Tighten this wording"}]}' | hunk session comment apply --repo . --stdin
```

- `comment list --type user` shows human-authored inline notes; without `--type`, `comment list` preserves the legacy live-agent-comment view
- `comment add` is best for one note; `comment apply` is best when an agent already has several notes ready
- `comment add` requires `--file`, `--summary`, and exactly one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`
- `comment apply` payload items require `filePath`, `summary`, and exactly one target such as `hunk`, `hunkNumber`, `oldLine`, or `newLine`
- `comment apply` reads a JSON batch from stdin and validates the full batch before mutating the live session
- Pass `--focus` when you want to jump to the new note or the first note in a batch
- `comment list` and `comment clear` accept optional `--file`
- Quote `--summary` and `--rationale` defensively in the shell

### Attention marks

Highlights paint character ranges inside the diff lines the user is looking at — use them to light up the exact expression you are explaining while you narrate.

```bash
hunk session highlight add (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) --start <n> --end <n> [--tone <tone>] [--focus] [--json]
hunk session highlight clear (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--json]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session highlight add --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 42 --start 6 --end 19
hunk session highlight add --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 42 --start 6 --end 19 --tone warning --focus
hunk session highlight clear --repo .
```

- `highlight add` requires `--file`, exactly one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`, and the `--start` / `--end` offsets
- `--start` is a 0-based inclusive offset into the line's text and `--end` is exclusive, counted in UTF-16 code units — the same `[start, end)` range extensions use
- Tones: `match` (default), `info`, `warning`, `error`; `current` renders as reverse video and is best reserved for the one range under discussion
- Pass `--focus` to also land the viewport on the marked line
- Marks survive scrolling, navigation, and reloads that leave the marked file's content unchanged; a reload that changes that file drops its marks, and `highlight clear` removes them explicitly (optionally per `--file`)
- Marks are visual only — pair them with a `comment add` when the explanation should persist as a note

### Experimental rich markup notes (STML)

Only use STML when `hunk session context --json` lists `stml` in `experimentalFeatures`. The user opts into that experience by launching the review with `--experimental`; do not ask a normal session to render markup.

For an opted-in session, `--markup` (or a `markup` field on apply items) renders the note body as STML — a small HTML-like markup for terminal UI (boxes, rows, gauges, badges, lists, code). Keep `--summary` a real sentence: it is the fallback and the `comment list` text.

Before writing markup, run `hunk markup guide` once — it has copy-paste patterns and the width rules. The session context also reports `noteMarkupWidth` (the live render width); preview with `hunk markup render - --width <that>`. Comment responses echo `markupWidth` and return `markupNotes` when markup degraded — fix what they flag.

## New files in working-tree reviews

`hunk diff` includes untracked files by default. If the user wants tracked changes only, reload with `--exclude-untracked`:

```bash
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff --exclude-untracked
```

## Guiding a review

The user may ask you to walk them through a changeset or review code using Hunk. Start with `hunk session review --json` to understand the file/hunk structure without inflating agent context, then use `--include-patch` only for the files you truly need to read in raw diff form. Use `context` and `navigate` to line up the user's current view before adding comments.

Your role is to narrate: steer the user's view to what matters and leave comments that explain what they're looking at.

Typical flow:

1. Load the right content (`reload` if needed)
2. Navigate to the first interesting file / hunk
3. Add a comment explaining what's happening and why
4. If you already have several notes ready, prefer one `comment apply` batch over many separate shell invocations
5. Summarize when done

Guidelines:

- Work in the order that tells the clearest story, not necessarily file order
- Navigate before commenting so the user sees the code you're discussing
- Use `highlight add --focus` to steer the user's eyes to the exact expression while you explain it, and `highlight clear` before moving to the next topic
- Use `comment apply` for agent-generated batches and `comment add` for one-off notes

- `--repo <path>` -- match the live session by its current loaded repo root (most common)
- `<session-id>` -- match by exact ID (use when multiple sessions share a repo)

- `--source <path>` -- load the replacement `diff` / `show` command from a different directory

Use `--source` only for advanced reloads where the live session you want to control is not already associated with the checkout you want to load next. For a normal worktree session, prefer selecting it directly with `--repo /path/to/worktree`.

## Commands

### Inspect

```bash
hunk session list [--json]
hunk session get (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--json]
hunk session context (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--json]
hunk session review (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--include-patch] [--include-notes] [--json]
```

- `get` shows the session `Path`, `Repo`, and `Source`, which helps when choosing between `--repo` and `--session-path`
- `Repo` is what `--repo` matches; `Path` is what `--session-path` matches
- `review --json` returns file and hunk structure by default; add `--include-patch` only when a caller truly needs raw unified diff text
- `review --include-notes` also returns the live review notes alongside the file and hunk structure

### Navigate

```bash
hunk session navigate (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--hunk <n> | --old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) [--json]
hunk session navigate (<session-id> | --repo <path>) (--next-comment | --prev-comment) [--json]
```

Absolute navigation requires `--file` and exactly one of `--hunk`, `--new-line`, or `--old-line`:

```bash
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --hunk 2
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 372
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --old-line 355
```

Relative comment navigation jumps between annotated hunks and does not require `--file`:

```bash
hunk session navigate --repo . --next-comment
hunk session navigate --repo . --prev-comment
```

- `--hunk <n>` is 1-based
- `--new-line` / `--old-line` are 1-based line numbers on that diff side
- A line target lands the user's viewport on that exact line (falling back to its hunk when the line is inside a collapsed region); `--hunk` lands on the hunk
- Use either `--next-comment` or `--prev-comment`, not both

### Reload

Swaps the live session's contents. Pass a Hunk review command after `--`:

```bash
hunk session reload (<session-id> | --repo <path> | --session-path <path>) [--source <path>] [--json] -- diff [ref] [-- <pathspec...>]
hunk session reload (<session-id> | --repo <path> | --session-path <path>) [--source <path>] [--json] -- show [ref] [-- <pathspec...>]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff main...feature -- src/ui
hunk session reload --repo . -- show HEAD~1
hunk session reload --repo . -- show HEAD~1 -- README.md
hunk session reload --repo /path/to/worktree -- diff
hunk session reload --session-path /path/to/live-window --source /path/to/other-checkout -- diff
```

- Always include `--` before the nested Hunk command
- `--repo` or `<session-id>` usually selects the session you want
- `--source` is advanced: it does not select the session; it only changes where the replacement review command runs
- If the live session is already showing the target worktree, prefer `hunk session reload --repo /path/to/worktree -- diff`
- `--session-path` targets the live window when you need to keep session selection separate from reload source

### Comments

```bash
hunk session comment add (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) --summary <text> [--rationale <text>] [--author <name>] [--markup <stml>] [--focus] [--json]
hunk session comment apply (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --stdin [--focus] [--json]
hunk session comment list (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--type <live|all|ai|agent|user>] [--json]
hunk session comment rm (<session-id> | --repo <path>) <comment-id> [--json]
hunk session comment clear (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--include-user|--all] --yes [--json]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session comment add --repo . --file README.md --new-line 103 --summary "Tighten this wording"
printf '%s\n' '{"comments":[{"filePath":"README.md","newLine":103,"summary":"Tighten this wording"}]}' | hunk session comment apply --repo . --stdin
```

- `comment list --type user` shows human-authored inline notes; without `--type`, `comment list` preserves the legacy live-agent-comment view
- `comment add` is best for one note; `comment apply` is best when an agent already has several notes ready
- `comment add` requires `--file`, `--summary`, and exactly one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`
- `comment apply` payload items require `filePath`, `summary`, and exactly one target such as `hunk`, `hunkNumber`, `oldLine`, or `newLine`
- `comment apply` reads a JSON batch from stdin and validates the full batch before mutating the live session
- Pass `--focus` when you want to jump to the new note or the first note in a batch
- `comment list` and `comment clear` accept optional `--file`
- Quote `--summary` and `--rationale` defensively in the shell

### Attention marks

Highlights paint character ranges inside the diff lines the user is looking at — use them to light up the exact expression you are explaining while you narrate.

```bash
hunk session highlight add (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) --start <n> --end <n> [--tone <tone>] [--focus] [--json]
hunk session highlight clear (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--json]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session highlight add --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 42 --start 6 --end 19
hunk session highlight add --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 42 --start 6 --end 19 --tone warning --focus
hunk session highlight clear --repo .
```

- `highlight add` requires `--file`, exactly one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`, and the `--start` / `--end` offsets
- `--start` is a 0-based inclusive offset into the line's text and `--end` is exclusive, counted in UTF-16 code units — the same `[start, end)` range extensions use
- Tones: `match` (default), `info`, `warning`, `error`; `current` renders as reverse video and is best reserved for the one range under discussion

- Marks survive scrolling, navigation, and reloads that leave the marked file's content unchanged; a reload that changes that file drops its marks, and `highlight clear` removes them explicitly (optionally per `--file`)
- Marks are visual only — pair them with a `comment add` when the explanation should persist as a note

### Experimental rich markup notes (STML)

Only use STML when `hunk session context --json` lists `stml` in `experimentalFeatures`. The user opts into that experience by launching the review with `--experimental`; do not ask a normal session to render markup.

For an opted-in session, `--markup` (or a `markup` field on apply items) renders the note body as STML — a small HTML-like markup for terminal UI (boxes, rows, gauges, badges, lists, code). Keep `--summary` a real sentence: it is the fallback and the `comment list` text.

Before writing markup, run `hunk markup guide` once — it has copy-paste patterns and the width rules. The session context also reports `noteMarkupWidth` (the live render width); preview with `hunk markup render - --width <that>`. Comment responses echo `markupWidth` and return `markupNotes` when markup degraded — fix what they flag.

## New files in working-tree reviews

`hunk diff` includes untracked files by default. If the user wants tracked changes only, reload with `--exclude-untracked`:

```bash
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff --exclude-untracked
```

## Guiding a review

The user may ask you to walk them through a changeset or review code using Hunk. Start with `hunk session review --json` to understand the file/hunk structure without inflating agent context, then use `--include-patch` only for the files you truly need to read in raw diff form. Use `context` and `navigate` to line up the user's current view before adding comments.

Your role is to narrate: steer the user's view to what matters and leave comments that explain what they're looking at.

Typical flow:

1. Load the right content (`reload` if needed)
2. Navigate to the first interesting file / hunk
3. Add a comment explaining what's happening and why
4. If you already have several notes ready, prefer one `comment apply` batch over many separate shell invocations
5. Summarize when done

Guidelines:

- Work in the order that tells the clearest story, not necessarily file order
- Navigate before commenting so the user sees the code you're discussing
- Use `highlight add --focus` to steer the user's eyes to the exact expression while you explain it, and `highlight clear` before moving to the next topic
- Use `comment apply` for agent-generated batches and `comment add` for one-off notes
- Use `--focus` sparingly when the note itself should actively steer the review
- Keep comments focused: intent, structure, risks, or follow-ups
- Don't comment on every hunk -- highlight what the user wouldn't spot themselves

## Common errors

- **"No diff file matches ..."** -- the file is not in the loaded review. Check `context`, then `reload` if needed.
- **"No active Hunk sessions"** -- if Hunk is visibly running, localhost may be blocked by the agent sandbox; retry with network/sandbox escalation. Otherwise ask the user to open Hunk.
- **"Multiple active sessions match"** -- pass `<session-id>` explicitly.
- **"No active session matches session path ..."** -- for advanced split-path reloads, verify the live window `Path` via `hunk session get` or `list`, then use `--session-path`.
- **"Pass the replacement Hunk command after `--`"** -- include `--` before the nested `diff` / `show` command.
- **"Pass --stdin to read batch comments from stdin JSON."** -- `comment apply` only reads its batch payload from stdin.
- **"Specify exactly one navigation target"** -- pick one of `--hunk`, `--old-line`, or `--new-line`.
- **"Specify exactly one comment target"** -- pass `comment add` one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`.
- **"Specify exactly one highlight target"** -- pass `highlight add` one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`.
- **"Highlight --end must be greater than --start"** -- offsets are `[start, end)` UTF-16 code units into the line text; end is exclusive.
- **"Specify either --next-comment or --prev-comment, not both."** -- choose one comment-navigation direction.
- **"Could not read the raw diff for ..."** -- the session reloaded or closed while `--include-patch` was reading it. Re-run `review`; drop `--include-patch` if you only need file and hunk structure.

---
name: herdr
description: "Control Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Use only when the user explicitly mentions Herdr or asks to use Herdr to inspect or control panes, tabs, workspaces, commands, or another agent. Do not use merely because a task could benefit from a background terminal, delegation, or parallel work. Requires HERDR_ENV=1."
---

# Herdr

Herdr organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, recognizes coding agents running inside panes, and exposes the current session through the `herdr` CLI.

Before issuing any control command, verify that this agent is running inside a Herdr-managed pane:

```bash
test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1
```

If the check fails, say that you are not running inside Herdr and stop. Do not inspect or control the focused Herdr session from outside Herdr.

When the check passes, the `herdr` binary in `PATH` talks to the current session. Use it to inspect neighboring work, create terminal layout, start agents and commands, read output, and wait for state changes.

## Learn the current CLI

The installed binary is the authority for command syntax. Start with:

```bash
herdr --help
```

Then print the relevant command group by running the group without a subcommand:

```bash
herdr agent
herdr pane
herdr workspace
herdr tab
herdr worktree
herdr terminal
herdr notification
herdr integration
herdr session
```

Do not run bare `herdr` for discovery; it launches or attaches the TUI. Do not probe a mutating nested command by omitting arguments. Commands such as `herdr workspace create` are valid with defaults and will execute.

Most control commands return JSON. Read identifiers and state from those responses instead of predicting them.

## Understand layout, panes, and agents

Choose the primitive that matches the job:

- Workspace, tab, and pane topology organize terminal locations.
- Pane commands control raw terminals, shells, tests, servers, input, and output.
- Agent commands control the recognized coding agent currently occupying a pane.

A pane exists whether or not it contains an agent. `agent start` requires an existing available shell pane and never creates, splits, or moves layout. Use pane commands for ordinary processes. Use agent commands when Herdr must validate agent identity or interpret `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, and `unknown` lifecycle states.

Agent commands accept either a unique live agent name or the pane ID currently hosting that agent. They do not accept terminal IDs or bare agent-kind labels. Names must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}` and be unique among live agents. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced.

`idle` means the agent is ready for input and its tab has been seen in the focused Herdr UI. `done` is the same underlying idle state after unseen background work finishes. Focusing the tab or targeting the pane or agent with a focus command marks it seen. CLI reads do not mark it seen. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently; it does not prove completion.

## Use IDs and caller context

Public IDs are opaque stable handles:

- workspace: `w1`
- tab: `w1:t1`
- pane: `w1:p1`

Closed tab and pane IDs are not reused. A pane moved into another workspace receives a new workspace-qualified pane ID. After `pane move`, continue with `.result.move_result.pane.pane_id` or the live agent name. The old value is reported as `.result.move_result.previous_pane_id`; only the moved process's inherited caller context keeps resolving that old ID, so do not use it as a general agent target.

Herdr injects the caller's context into each managed pane:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID" "$HERDR_TAB_ID" "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Prefer `--current` when a pane command should target the calling pane. Omitting a target may use the UI-focused pane, which can belong to the user or another client.

Discover live state with:

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr tab list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr pane current --current
herdr pane list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr agent list
```

Creation responses expose the IDs to use next. `workspace create` returns `.result.workspace`, `.result.tab`, and `.result.root_pane`. `tab create` returns `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`. `pane split` returns the new pane as `.result.pane`.

## Start and coordinate an agent

Default to a sibling pane in the current tab and the current working directory. Do not create a workspace, tab, worktree, or different cwd unless the user explicitly requests that topology or location.

Honor a direction requested by the user. Otherwise inspect the caller pane:

```bash
herdr pane layout --pane "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Split a wide pane to the right and a narrow or tall pane down. Avoid repeated same-direction splits that create unusably narrow columns or short rows. Keep the user's focus in the calling pane and explicitly preserve the caller's working directory:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Replace `right` with `down` when appropriate. Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`.

An available shell pane must be at its interactive prompt, with the shell itself in the foreground and no foreground command, editor, or agent running. Start a supported agent in that pane with a useful unique name:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id>
```

Use the kind requested by the user. Run `herdr agent` to inspect the installed kind list and options. Pass native agent arguments only after `--`:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id> -- <agent-args...>
```

A successful `agent start` returns only after Herdr detects the expected agent in the same pane and considers it ready for interactive input. If the agent is blocked during startup, the command returns `agent_not_ready` immediately but keeps the name available for `agent read` and `agent send-keys`. Wait until the agent becomes idle before prompting it. Startup defaults to a 30-second timeout.

Submit work through the agent surface:

```bash
herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff and report only actionable findings." --wait --timeout 120000
```

`agent prompt` honors the pane's live bracketed-paste mode and sends text followed by encoded Enter after a short delay. It rejects an agent already waiting at an approval or question dialog with `agent_blocked` before sending any input. Inspect the blocked UI and ask the user before answering it. For normal agent work, `--wait` is enough: it waits for the first settled `idle`, `done`, or `blocked` state. Do not repeat those defaults with `--until`.

A prompt sent from a non-working state must produce an observed lifecycle change within five seconds. Otherwise Herdr returns `agent_prompt_stalled` instead of waiting indefinitely. This wait tracks lifecycle state, not an individual turn; if the agent is already working, completion of the active turn may satisfy it.

Use `--until` only for a state-specific workflow, such as waiting for an already-running agent to request input:

```bash
herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked --timeout 120000
```

Without `--until`, standalone `agent wait` uses the same settled-state defaults as `agent prompt --wait`.

Use logical keys for interactive agent UI controls:

```bash
herdr agent send-keys reviewer esc
herdr agent send-keys reviewer ctrl+c
```

Herdr validates all keys before writing any bytes. Read the result through the resolved agent:

```bash
herdr agent get reviewer
herdr agent read reviewer --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

If a wait fails or returns `blocked`, inspect `agent get` and `agent read` before deciding what input to send. Use the pane surface only when raw terminal control is intentional.

## Run an ordinary command in another pane

Create a sibling pane with the same geometry rule, preserve the caller's working directory, and keep user focus unchanged:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`, then run and inspect the command:

```bash
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "just test"
herdr pane wait-output <returned-pane-id> --match "test result" --timeout 120000
herdr pane read <returned-pane-id> --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

`pane run` atomically sends command text and Enter. `pane wait-output` searches the selected snapshot immediately, so output that already exists can match. Use `--match <text>` for a literal substring or `--regex <pattern>` for a Rust regular expression. Omitting `--timeout` allows an indefinite wait.

Use the read source that matches the task:

- `visible`: the currently rendered viewport.
- `recent`: recent rendered output, including soft wraps.
- `recent-unwrapped`: recent output with soft wraps joined; prefer it for logs and transcripts.
- `detection`: the plain-text bottom-buffer snapshot used for agent detection.

Use `--format ansi` when colors and terminal styling are evidence. Otherwise use text.

`--lines` asks Herdr for more rows from the pane's available screen and host scrollback. If increasing it does not reveal more of a completed response, the pane is probably running the agent on the terminal's alternate screen. Rows that leave the alternate screen do not enter Herdr's host scrollback, so a larger line count cannot recover them.

After that failed read, ask the agent to write its complete response as Markdown in a temporary directory and reply only with the file path, then read the file directly. Use this only as a fallback; do not request file output in the initial prompt.

## Safety and coordination rules

- Use `--no-focus` for background work unless the user asked to switch context.
- Use `--current`, an explicit pane ID, or a unique agent name. Do not rely on another client's focused pane.
- Parse IDs from JSON responses. Do not derive them from sidebar order or examples.
- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes, or sessions you did not create unless the user explicitly asked.
- Never run `herdr server stop` from an active session unless the user explicitly intends to stop the server and its pane processes.
- Never kill the main Herdr process. Use named test sessions for experiments that need an isolated server.
- CLI server errors are JSON on stderr with exit status 1. CLI syntax errors exit with status 2.

Herdr organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, recognizes coding agents running inside panes, and exposes the current session through the `herdr` CLI.

Choose the primitive that matches the job:

- Pane commands control raw terminals, shells, tests, servers, input, and output.
- Agent commands control the recognized coding agent currently occupying a pane.

Use agent commands when Herdr must validate agent identity or interpret `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, and `unknown` lifecycle states.

Agent commands accept either a unique live agent name or the pane ID currently hosting that agent. They do not accept terminal IDs or bare agent-kind labels. Names must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}` and be unique among live agents. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced.

`idle` means the agent is ready for input and its tab has been seen in the focused Herdr UI. `done` is the same underlying idle state after unseen background work finishes. Focusing the tab or targeting the pane or agent with a focus command marks it seen. CLI reads do not mark it seen. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently; it does not prove completion.

Public IDs are opaque stable handles:

- workspace: `w1`
- tab: `w1:t1`
- pane: `w1:p1`

<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/Users/pfleidi/.agents/skills`
- `r1` = `/Users/pfleidi/.codex/skills/.system`
- `r2` = `/Users/pfleidi/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-curated-remote`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r1/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r1/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- plugin-creator: Create and scaffold plugin directories for Codex with a required `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, optional plugin folders/files, valid manifest defaults, and personal-marketplace entries by default. Use when Codex needs to create a new personal plugin, add optional plugin structure, generate or update marketplace entries for plugin ordering and availability metadata, or update an existing local plugin during development with the CLI-driven cachebuster and reinstall flow. (file: r1/plugin-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r1/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r1/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- context7-mcp: This skill should be used when the user asks about libraries, frameworks, API references, or needs code examples. Activates for setup questions, code generation involving libraries, or mentions of specific frameworks like React, Vue, Next.js, Prisma, Supabase, etc. (file: r0/context7-mcp/SKILL.md)
- deslop: Remove AI-generated code slop and clean up code style (file: r0/deslop/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:clean-go: Review changed Go code against origin/main using modern Go and local conventions. Use for Go cleanliness or refactoring review. Remains read-only unless the user explicitly asks to apply fixes. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/clean-go/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:daily-status: Use when the user asks for a daily Slack status, standup update, work recap, report since a previous update, or a summary of recent Linear, authored GitHub PR, Entire trail, completed personal daily-board tasks, and work-related Slack activity. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/daily-status/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:de-slop: Use when the user asks to de-slop, simplify code, remove cruft, reduce over-abstraction, clean up weak tests, simplify a current branch or named code area, or explicitly invokes pfleidi:de-slop. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/de-slop/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:explain-diff: Use when the user asks for a rich explanation, teaching-style walkthrough, or shareable writeup of a code change, diff, branch, commit, or PR — e.g. "explain this diff", "help me understand this PR", "make an explainer for this change" — or invokes /explain-diff. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/explain-diff/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:feedback: Use when the user asks to fix, address, explain, triage, respond to, dismiss, resolve, publish, or watch remote review feedback for the current branch; mentions Bugbot, Copilot, GitHub PR comments, or Entire trail findings; or invokes /feedback or pfleidi:feedback. Also collects read-only local findings alongside remote intake. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/feedback/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:guided-research: Use when the user asks for guided research, deep research, codebase understanding, a coworker-readable research artifact, answers to annotated research docs, or live watching of a Markdown research artifact. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/guided-research/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:human-review: Run a synchronous local human review in Hunk for one implementation slice, a complete branch diff, or an uncommitted feedback fix batch. Use only when the user explicitly asks to inspect code in Hunk, leave Hunk comments, or invokes human-review. Do not activate for a generic review request or merely because changes are ready to commit. Opens Hunk in the implementation workspace when Herdr is active; never commits or pushes. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/human-review/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:investigate-alert: Use when the user provides a Datadog monitor URL/ID, Datadog event URL, pasted alert text, incident, or monitor name and asks whether it is noise, why it fired, how to investigate it, how to tune it, or invokes /investigate-alert. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/investigate-alert/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:pr: Use when the user wants to create, open, or make a GitHub pull request for the current branch, asks to prepare the branch for PR creation, provides an optional PR target base branch, or invokes /pr. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/pr/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:project-shape: Use when the user wants to investigate, define, or substantially restructure a multi-issue engineering project; turn a parent issue into thin vertical slices; identify spikes, dependencies, parallel work, risks, or completion criteria; or invokes project-shape. Do not use for a routine morning project reconciliation when project-update applies. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/project-shape/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:project-update: Use for a fast morning or recurring update of an existing multi-issue engineering project: reconcile child issues and native relationships with current pull-request, blocker, rollout, and validation state; propose tracker corrections; prioritize the next five meaningful steps; and publish the next appropriate user-owned actions for concrete work items to the fixed daily kanban-md board by default. Do not use for initial project design or substantial restructuring when project-shape applies. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/project-update/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:remote-review: Use when the user asks for local feedback on a GitHub PR or Entire trail, provides a PR/trail URL or number, asks to review an Entire trail, asks for PR/trail feedback without fixing it, or explicitly invokes pfleidi:remote-review. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/remote-review/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:review: Review the current branch and working tree against origin/main, validate concrete findings, and report merge-relevant issues. Use for local code or documentation review before merge. Remains read-only unless the user explicitly asks to apply fixes. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/review/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:task-align: Guide the user through evidence-backed brainstorming for one Linear or GitHub task before execution: build a shared system model, separate facts from proposals, explore material options and tradeoffs, let the user settle the decisions, and define development and post-deploy validation. Use when issue-derived work has unclear evidence, scope, behavior, risk, or validation, or when task-implement requests alignment. Skip clear, small tasks with no material decisions. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/task-align/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:task-implement: Start and implement one well-scoped Linear or GitHub task: align it when needed, update native tracker state, run no-code work in a coordinator-workspace tab, or create an Entire worktree and focused implementation session that aligns only when needed before editing. Use Herdr when active; otherwise use the invoking session. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/task-implement/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:task-validate: Guide a human through end-to-end validation of one implemented Linear or GitHub task from a user perspective. When Herdr is active, open a right-hand split shell for the human, prepare the prerequisites and validation steps, walk through them interactively, and help diagnose issues. Use the current task-workspace agent without spawning another agent or isolated worktree, and do not substitute code review or pfleidi:feedback for human validation. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/task-validate/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:testing: Local testing strategy and review guidance for meaningful tests, choosing unit vs integration vs end-to-end scope, avoiding production-only test seams and over-mocking, and keeping test helpers readable, especially in Go. Use when writing, changing, or reviewing tests; adding mocks or test helpers; deciding test scope; or when user mentions pfleidi:testing. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/testing/SKILL.md)
- plugin-management:plugin-management: Discover and suggest relevant plugins, inspect app permissions and dependencies, and manage plugin connections or removal. Use when the user asks about plugins or when a task would materially benefit from an external app, account, service, or data source that available tools cannot access. (file: r2/plugin-management/0.1.0/skills/plugin-management/SKILL.md)
- search: Use when the user wants to find prior work, checkpoints, or agent conversations by topic, repo, branch, author, or recent time window, or to search code content across repositories (file: r0/search/SKILL.md)
- using-entire: Use when codebase exploration or explanation would benefit from historical implementation intent recorded in Entire checkpoints. Combines current source with checkpoint evidence without treating unavailable history as a blocker. (file: r0/using-entire/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions>

---
name: feedback
description: >
  Use when the user asks to fix, address, explain, triage, respond to,
  dismiss, resolve, publish, or watch remote review feedback for the current
  branch; mentions Bugbot, Copilot, GitHub PR comments, or Entire trail
  findings; or invokes /feedback or pfleidi:feedback. Also collects read-only
  local findings alongside remote intake.
---

# Feedback

Coordinate read-only local analysis, Bugbot, Copilot, and Entire feedback for
the current checkout. Within this feedback cycle, this coordinator is the only
participant allowed to modify the working tree. Read
`../review/references/analysis-only.md`, `references/github.md`, and
`references/entire.md` before intake. Read
[the remote-sentinel reference](references/remote-sentinel.md) only when the
concurrent topology below selects it.

## 1. Establish the current branch

1. Run `git branch --show-current`. Stop on an empty result: detached HEAD is not eligible.
2. Record the branch, `git rev-parse HEAD`, and `git status --short` before remote intake. Treat existing changes as user-owned unless the user identifies them otherwise.
3. Parse optional PR and trail selectors without checking out a branch or creating a worktree. Give each selector to its provider reference for repository and branch validation.
4. Stop without remote processing when an explicit selector does not match the current repository or checked-out branch. State the selector, current branch, and mismatch. Never switch branches.

## 2. Start review intake

1. Treat the recorded local `HEAD` as the candidate commit. In one initial
   phase, inspect its changed surface just enough to choose the analysis-only
   review intensity, set the GitHub provider's one- or two-round automated
   review budget, and perform GitHub and Entire discovery plus selector
   validation. Do not launch review agents yet.
2. Use only each provider's documented retry. After a failed retry of discovery
   or another core read, retain the exact failure, mark that provider
   unavailable, and continue other sources. A missing PR or trail makes only
   that provider unavailable. Stop only for an explicit selector mismatch or
   when neither remote provider is available.
3. When both GitHub and Entire are available, local analysis needs parallel
   review, and runtime capacity can retain at least two local review agents
   after reserving one slot, launch exactly one remote sentinel using its
   reference. Otherwise keep remote intake in the coordinator: start any
   available Entire watcher as a background process, wait for `ready`, and run
   GitHub intake concurrently with local analysis. Never spend the only
   available local review slot on a sentinel.
4. With a sentinel, wait for `REMOTE_READY`; without one, wait for the
   coordinator-owned watcher to become ready or enter its documented fallback.
   Then start local analysis and any warranted GitHub reviewer requests in the
   same orchestration phase. The sentinel uses the remaining time to monitor
   both remote providers while local review agents run. The coordinator owns
   reviewer requests because they are provider writes.
5. Run the analysis-only review against the immutable candidate. A dirty
   working tree does not change the candidate or block this read-only analysis;
   retain it as user-owned state for later applicability and overlap checks.
   Parallel analysis uses the capacity left after the sentinel; combine lenses
   as the review reference directs, and have the coordinator cover a remaining
   relevant lens when useful. A local-analysis failure does not block GitHub or
   Entire.
6. After initial intake, compare the candidate with the PR's `headRefOid` and
   retain both revisions as provenance. A mismatch does not discard findings or
   block work. Re-read the relevant current local source and decide whether
   each local or remote finding still applies before classification or editing.
7. Refresh PR identity and `headRefOid` immediately before reviewer requests
   and every later request, edit, commit/push, or publish phase. Do not require
   local `HEAD`, the starting candidate, and `headRefOid` to be equal. Before
   editing, refresh the local working-tree state, preserve user-owned changes,
   and skip an item whose fix would overlap them unsafely. Stop only if the
   repository or checked-out branch no longer identifies the selected PR or
   trail.
8. Follow the GitHub provider's reviewer-request criteria and round budget. A
   review from an earlier commit remains usable input when its findings can be
   checked against current code; commit inequality or a new push alone does not
   require a new review. Do not duplicate an `In flight` reviewer. A
   reviewer-specific failure marks only that reviewer unavailable.
9. Run local analysis only for the starting candidate. After this coordinator
   pushes its own fixes, focused verification covers those fixes while remote
   reviewers are refreshed against the new head.

## 3. Collect the candidate review before editing

Do not edit or publish while review sources are collecting findings. Merge
`REMOTE_READY` and `REMOTE_DELTA` records into the candidate queue while local
analysis runs. Without a sentinel, refresh GitHub and Entire from the
coordinator-owned watcher as before.

After local analysis and every reviewer request started by this run completes
or becomes unavailable, send `FINALIZE` to the sentinel. Wait for
`REMOTE_FINAL`, including confirmation that its watcher stopped, before
freezing the queue. Without a sentinel, the coordinator performs the same final
refresh and quiet-window work itself.

The remote owner snapshots reviewer state, unresolved/open sets, and newest
timestamps, then starts a 60-second quiet window. It refreshes at the end and
for every watcher event. Reset the window only when an authoritative state or
timestamp changes; duplicate, reconnect, error, or unfamiliar watcher events
alone do not reset it.

A completed `Stale` review is provenance, not an automatic blocker: collect its
findings and validate them against current code. `Missing` is a coverage gap,
and `In flight` remains unsettled. An unavailable source does not block useful
work but prevents an unqualified comprehensive result. Cap collection at 15
minutes. At the cap, stop an unfinished local analysis and mark it timed out,
process the complete findings collected so far, and leave unsettled items open.

If local `HEAD`, the working tree, or the PR head changes during collection,
refresh the affected source and re-evaluate queued findings. Do not stop solely
because a SHA changed, and do not combine findings from different revisions
until current-source evidence confirms the same underlying issue.

## 4. Normalize and group feedback

1. Build one queue from confirmed local Required findings, unresolved Bugbot
   and Copilot threads, feedback-bearing top-level bot results, Entire
   open/current findings, and relevant human discussion. Retain local sources
   and evidence plus every remote identifier and status needed for publication.
   Keep local Improvements and dismissed candidates in the report, outside the
   fix queue.
2. Treat unknown remote authors as human-owned.
3. Group reports only after reading current source and confirming one underlying
   failure on the same code path. Findings may originate from different
   revisions; similar wording or matching SHAs are insufficient.
4. A grouped issue has one local fix. Retain every local source and remote ID;
   publish updates independently after a successful push.

## 5. Present human feedback

Before editing, present every human, maintainer, and unknown-author item verbatim. For each item include its provider, location, author, stable ID, source-backed relevance assessment, current-code evidence, and the exact manual decision or in-person follow-up required.

Human feedback remains user-owned. Do not edit code, reply, resolve, dismiss, or otherwise publish an action for it unless the user explicitly selects that exact item after this presentation. Its unresolved status does not block independent automated work.

## 6. Classify automated feedback

For each automated item, re-read current source and its full remote context when
one exists, then assign exactly one of these actions:

- `Autofix eligible`: automated, source-backed, high confidence, minimal, unambiguous, in scope, and verifiable without a new dependency or a shared contract decision.
- `Needs decision`: automated feedback involving product behavior, public or shared interfaces, dependencies, schemas, broad refactors, test-scope changes, unclear intent, or multiple reasonable fixes.
- `Dismissible`: automated feedback proven stale, invalid, already addressed, or duplicated.

For `Needs decision`, present a decision brief with the verbatim request, plain-language problem, current-code and review-context evidence, the gain and risk of leaving it unchanged, the gain, verification, and design cost of changing it, and the exact decision needed. Do not publish a judgment-based rejection without user-provided public rationale. Continue with independent `Autofix eligible` items.

Any finding that would change product behavior, component ownership, data or
control flow, a public/shared interface, persistence, or an agreed invariant is
`Needs decision`. Return it to the synchronous development workflow; do not let
the asynchronous review cycle revise the user's system model silently.

Local Improvements remain report-only and do not enter this action
classification.

Treat a request to rewrite or broaden useful unit tests as `Needs decision` unless source review proves the missing boundary needs a narrow additive integration or end-to-end test. Preserve useful unit tests.

Classify a remote automated item as already addressed without a code change only
after verifying that the relevant fix exists in that provider's pushed branch
head. A fix present only in the working tree, index, or an unpushed commit is not
already addressed: keep the item open and route it through verification plus the
commit/push gate before publishing.

## 7. Apply one fix queue

1. Freeze the collected queue for this fix batch and process grouped `Autofix
   eligible` issues sequentially. Review sources stay read-only; only this
   coordinator mutates files. Late items wait for the next intake or final
   report.
2. Before each edit, refresh every linked remote item when one exists and
   re-read affected source. Confirm the finding remains current, in scope, and
   does not overlap user-owned changes. Skip unsafe overlap and report it.
3. Decide whether the issue is local or systemic, then apply the narrowest correct fix. Do not add dependencies, change shared/public interfaces, or make product/design choices without the user's decision.
4. For behavior changes, add or update directly related tests in the same batch and complete a focused red-to-green cycle. Record changed files and the verification required for every linked ID.
5. Use an Entire suggested patch only after its provider check succeeds and this coordinator has confirmed the patch is minimal and source-backed.

## 8. Verify once per final changed surface

1. After the final fix batch, run focused build, lint, and tests for the combined changed surface. Reuse a non-stale equivalent result instead of duplicating it.
2. When a fix changes SQL, query-builder use, or migrations, statically validate it against the current schema and call path, parameter bindings, transaction/error/result behavior, and repository-provided SQL tooling when available. Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` only for a confirmed read-only query against local or development synthetic data. Never execute writes, migrations, production queries, or customer data for validation.
3. Record every command, exit status, and relevant output. If no code changed, skip code verification and state why.
4. When a required verification fails because of the fix, allow at most two focused repair rounds. If it still fails, report the failing command and output; do not commit, push, or publish code-fix statuses. Leave linked code-fix items open.
5. Do not call the result ready while required compile/build status is failing or unknown.

## 9. Commit and push gate

Do not invoke a review tool automatically. If the user explicitly asks to
review the uncommitted feedback fixes in Hunk, invoke `pfleidi:human-review`
with slice scope. Address only the exact current Hunk comments the user selects
after they are presented verbatim. If that review changes code, return to
section 8 and verify the final changed surface again before continuing.

When code changed and required verification passed, present one combined
summary: grouped issues, changed files, verification evidence, and the provider
IDs awaiting publication. Refresh local and remote branch state and confirm that
the selected PR still uses the checked-out branch; exact `HEAD` and `headRefOid`
equality is not required. Then ask once for approval to stage only
feedback-related changes, commit, and push.

Do not commit, push, reply to, resolve, or dismiss code-fix items without that approval and a successful push. Approval covers only the current fix batch; any later batch discovered after re-review requires a fresh commit-and-push approval. If the user declines, leave changes local, keep linked code-fix items open, and state this in the final report. Never force-push.

## 10. Publish provider updates

1. After a successful push, refresh `headRefOid` and verify that the current PR head contains the pushed fix commit and the relevant fix. Exact equality with local `HEAD` is not required because unrelated commits may have advanced the branch. If containment or the fix cannot be proved, leave the linked item open. Otherwise update every linked ID for each fixed grouped issue. Perform independent provider writes in parallel; preserve successful writes if another provider fails.
2. For GitHub, post the provider reference's direct reply with the specific change and commit, then resolve only after the reply succeeds. For Entire, resolve with the specific change and verification evidence.
3. For a `Dismissible` item, publish only a factual source-proven stale, invalid, already-addressed, or duplicate reason. No-code factual dismissals may publish without a commit. A duplicate linked to a code fix waits until that fix is pushed.
4. Keep human items, `Needs decision` items, ambiguous automated items, and unpushed code-fix items open. Return each successful update and exact failed operation/output.
5. After the provider-update attempts, refresh `headRefOid` and classify earlier
   Bugbot and Copilot reviews against it. Do not request another review merely
   because this push made them `Stale`. Lightweight and direct changes receive
   no post-push round. For a parallel full change, request a second round only
   when the GitHub provider's criteria justify it and the two-round budget has
   room. Never request a third round. When a permitted round starts, return to
   remote intake within the existing 15-minute active-loop cap. Do not repeat
   local analysis for coordinator-authored fixes. Preserve successful provider
   updates when another update or reviewer request fails; Entire continues
   independently after the GitHub budget is exhausted.

## 11. Final refresh and report

1. Ensure the owner of every Entire watcher stopped it and confirmed that it
   ended. Refresh each available provider one final time. The coordinator may
   use a new coordinator-owned watcher for post-push intake; never reuse a
   sentinel-owned watcher session after `REMOTE_FINAL`.
2. Report the candidate commit; local-analysis status and findings; the final
   `headRefOid`; the linked PR as `ID (title)`; provider availability and final
   status; the GitHub review rounds used and budget; every human item and
   required follow-up; grouped automated outcomes; verification; commit/push
   result; provider updates; late items; unsettled feedback; and exact failures.
3. Claim that no known actionable feedback remains only when local analysis
   completed, every fetched finding was checked against current source, no
   actionable local Required or open/current remote item remains, every review
   request started by this run settled, and the 60-second quiet window was
   unchanged. Report the revisions actually covered. A completed review does
   not become unusable merely because its SHA is older; `Missing`, `In flight`,
   or unavailable sources remain explicit coverage gaps. Otherwise state
   precisely what remains and why.

When a fix changes SQL, query-builder use, or migrations, statically validate it against the current schema and call path, parameter bindings, transaction/error/result behavior, and repository-provided SQL tooling when available. Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` only for a confirmed read-only query against local or development synthetic data. Never execute writes, migrations, production queries, or customer data for validation.
3. Record every command, exit status, and relevant output. If no code changed, skip code verification and state why.
4. When a required verification fails because of the fix, allow at most two focused repair rounds. If it still fails, report the failing command and output; do not commit, push, or publish code-fix statuses. Leave linked code-fix items open.
5. Do not call the result ready while required compile/build status is failing or unknown.

## 9. Commit and push gate

Do not invoke a review tool automatically. If the user explicitly asks to
review the uncommitted feedback fixes in Hunk, invoke `pfleidi:human-review`
with slice scope. Address only the exact current Hunk comments the user selects
after they are presented verbatim. If that review changes code, return to
section 8 and verify the final changed surface again before continuing.

When code changed and required verification passed, present one combined
summary: grouped issues, changed files, verification evidence, and the provider
IDs awaiting publication. Refresh local and remote branch state and confirm that
the selected PR still uses the checked-out branch; exact `HEAD` and `headRefOid`
equality is not required. Then ask once for approval to stage only
feedback-related changes, commit, and push.

Do not commit, push, reply to, resolve, or dismiss code-fix items without that approval and a successful push. Approval covers only the current fix batch; any later batch discovered after re-review requires a fresh commit-and-push approval. If the user declines, leave changes local, keep linked code-fix items open, and state this in the final report. Never force-push.

## 10. Publish provider updates

1. After a successful push, refresh `headRefOid` and verify that the current PR head contains the pushed fix commit and the relevant fix. Exact equality with local `HEAD` is not required because unrelated commits may have advanced the branch. If containment or the fix cannot be proved, leave the linked item open. Otherwise update every linked ID for each fixed grouped issue. Perform independent provider writes in parallel; preserve successful writes if another provider fails.
2. For GitHub, post the provider reference's direct reply with the specific change and commit, then resolve only after the reply succeeds. For Entire, resolve with the specific change and verification evidence.
3. For a `Dismissible` item, publish only a factual source-proven stale, invalid, already-addressed, or duplicate reason. No-code factual dismissals may publish without a commit. A duplicate linked to a code fix waits until that fix is pushed.
4. Keep human items, `Needs decision` items, ambiguous automated items, and unpushed code-fix items open. Return each successful update and exact failed operation/output.
5. After the provider-update attempts, refresh `headRefOid` and classify earlier
   Bugbot and Copilot reviews against it. Do not request another review merely
   because this push made them `Stale`. Lightweight and direct changes receive
   no post-push round. For a parallel full change, request a second round only
   when the GitHub provider's criteria justify it and the two-round budget has
   room. Never request a third round. When a permitted round starts, return to
   remote intake within the existing 15-minute active-loop cap. Do not repeat
   local analysis for coordinator-authored fixes. Preserve successful provider
   updates when another update or reviewer request fails; Entire continues
   independently after the GitHub budget is exhausted.

## 11. Final refresh and report

1. Ensure the owner of every Entire watcher stopped it and confirmed that it
   ended. Refresh each available provider one final time. The coordinator may
   use a new coordinator-owned watcher for post-push intake; never reuse a
   sentinel-owned watcher session after `REMOTE_FINAL`.
2. Report the candidate commit; local-analysis status and findings; the final
   `headRefOid`; the linked PR as `ID (title)`; provider availability and final
   status; the GitHub review rounds used and budget; every human item and
   required follow-up; grouped automated outcomes; verification; commit/push
   result; provider updates; late items; unsettled feedback; and exact failures.
3. Claim that no known actionable feedback remains only when local analysis
   completed, every fetched finding was checked against current source, no
   actionable local Required or open/current remote item remains, every review
   request started by this run settled, and the 60-second quiet window was
   unchanged. Report the revisions actually covered. A completed review does
   not become unusable merely because its SHA is older; `Missing`, `In flight`,
   or unavailable sources remain explicit coverage gaps. Otherwise state
   precisely what remains and why.

# Analysis-Only Review

Use this internal entry point only when another active skill requests a
read-only review of a named candidate commit.

## Pin The Candidate

Resolve the supplied candidate as a commit and use that object as the immutable
review snapshot. Record `git rev-parse HEAD` and `git status --short` only as
checkout context. Local `HEAD` may differ and the working tree may be dirty;
neither changes the named candidate or blocks a read-only review of it. Stop
only when the candidate cannot be resolved after the invoking workflow's
ordinary fetch or discovery step.

Review only:

```bash
git diff origin/main <candidate-commit> --stat
git diff origin/main <candidate-commit> --name-status
```

Use that candidate in path-scoped diffs as well. Do not substitute current
working-tree state, a merge base, local `main`, or a PR base. Confirm that the
candidate still resolves to the same commit before returning results. Do not
require it to match the checkout.

## Analyze Read-Only

Use lightweight intensity for documentation or low-risk metadata with no
runtime effect; direct intensity for a small cohesive code diff; and parallel
intensity for broad, high-risk, security, persistence, concurrency, migration,
generated-code, or shared/public-contract changes. For parallel intensity,
read [Parallel review](parallel-review.md). Do not edit files, create artifacts,
format, generate, update snapshots, run fix verification, commit, push, or read
or mutate remote provider state.

Check correctness, security boundaries, error paths, public contracts,
meaningful test coverage, needless complexity, and documentation/configuration
coherence as applicable to the diff. Validate every candidate against the
source before returning it.

Classify findings as Required or Improvement. Mark a Required item `Needs
decision` when it changes behavior, ownership, dependencies, schemas, or shared
interfaces; otherwise it may be `Eligible` for the invoking workflow to assess.
This classification does not authorize a fix.

Return the candidate commit, mode, stream status, confirmed findings, dismissed
candidates, and unavailable evidence to the invoking skill. Stop after the
report regardless of what was found.

# Entire provider

## Discovery and selector validation

Use only the named checked-out branch supplied by the coordinator. Never use a checkout or worktree command. Discover the current branch's trail with:

```bash
entire trail show
```

When the user supplied a trail selector, inspect it directly:

```bash
entire trail show TRAIL --repo TRAIL_REPO
git remote get-url origin
```

Verify that the returned trail repository is the current repository and its branch is the checked-out branch. Return a mismatch to the coordinator and stop intake if either differs.

Run every keychain-backed `entire trail ...` command with host/escalated permissions from the start in Codex: use `sandbox_permissions: require_escalated` for the exact command. Automatically retry an exact command at most once only when a read-only discovery, intake, or status read, or pre-ready watcher startup, fails because of authentication, permission, keychain, missing-session, forbidden, or suspicious network access. Do not inspect credentials or run login for the user. Retain the final command and output when the retry fails.

## Intake, refresh, and watcher

Assign exactly one watcher owner for each intake phase. The remote sentinel owns
the watcher when the feedback workflow selected one; otherwise the coordinator
owns it. Only that owner polls, writes to, interrupts, and confirms termination
of the watcher session. Follow [Remote feedback sentinel](remote-sentinel.md)
for its message and finalization contract.

Start the watcher before listing state and keep its session ID:

```bash
entire trail watch TRAIL --repo TRAIL_REPO --json
```

Require a `ready` event before treating realtime coverage as active. Use watcher events only as refresh triggers. On relevant finding or discussion events, reconnects, errors, or unfamiliar events, refresh the authoritative lists and report whether the unresolved/open sets or newest relevant timestamps changed.

If the watcher fails before `ready` because of authentication, permission, keychain, missing-session, forbidden, or suspicious network access, retry that exact watcher command once through the documented host/escalated path. If the initial pre-ready failure is not retry-eligible, or the eligible retry does not reach `ready`, use the watcher-failure fallback below. If a watcher that reached `ready` later fails, use the same fallback.

For any watcher-failure fallback, stop the watcher session and confirm it ended. Preserve every finding and discussion item already collected, report realtime coverage as unavailable, and continue with bounded authoritative list refreshes whenever the reads below work. A watcher failure alone does not make Entire unavailable: it remains in the queue, final refresh, and quiet-window snapshots while `trail show`, comment, and finding-list reads succeed. Mark Entire unavailable only when those authoritative reads fail after their allowed retry.

Fetch trail context and all current open feedback:

```bash
entire trail show TRAIL --repo TRAIL_REPO
entire trail approvals TRAIL --repo TRAIL_REPO --json
entire trail comment list --trail TRAIL --repo TRAIL_REPO --all --json
entire trail finding list TRAIL --repo TRAIL_REPO --status open --freshness current --json --limit 100
```

When the finding result reaches the limit, page with `--offset` until every open/current finding is present. Fetch details only when required for classification:

```bash
entire trail finding show TRAIL FINDING_ID --repo TRAIL_REPO
entire trail comment show THREAD_ID --trail TRAIL --repo TRAIL_REPO --json
```

Retain IDs, status, freshness, author, full text, location, suggested patch availability, and timestamps. Treat an unknown author as human-owned. After each coordinator boundary, drain watcher output, refresh the authoritative lists when triggered, and report whether they changed.

## Suggested patches and status updates

The coordinator alone decides eligibility and changes the working tree. It may first check an eligible suggested patch:

```bash
entire trail finding apply TRAIL FINDING_ID --repo TRAIL_REPO --check
```

Apply it only after that check succeeds and the coordinator confirms it remains eligible:

```bash
entire trail finding apply TRAIL FINDING_ID --repo TRAIL_REPO
```

Never pass `--resolve` to `finding apply`. Resolve a verified, pushed code fix with:

```bash
entire trail finding resolve TRAIL FINDING_ID --repo TRAIL_REPO -m "Addressed by <specific change>; verified with <command>."
```

Dismiss only a source-proven stale, invalid, already-addressed, or duplicate automated finding:

```bash
entire trail finding dismiss TRAIL FINDING_ID --repo TRAIL_REPO -m "<specific source-backed reason>."
```

Never blindly retry `finding apply`, resolve, or dismiss after an ambiguous failure. After an ambiguous apply failure, inspect the local diff and refresh the finding state before deciding whether any retry is safe. After an ambiguous resolve or dismiss failure, refresh the remote finding status before deciding whether any retry is safe.

The watcher owner must always interrupt it before returning and confirm the
session has ended. Return successful updates and exact failed
operations/output to the coordinator.

# GitHub provider

## Discovery and selector validation

Use the named checked-out branch supplied by the coordinator. Never switch branches. Discover only that branch's PR:

```bash
gh pr view --json number,title,body,url,headRefName,baseRefName,headRefOid
gh repo view --json nameWithOwner
```

Retain `nameWithOwner` as the checked-out repository's canonical GitHub identity. When the user supplied a PR number or URL, fetch its identity before intake:

```bash
gh pr view {selector} --json number,title,body,url,headRefName,baseRefName,headRefOid,headRepository,headRepositoryOwner
```

Read the selector URL and returned repository fields to identify the selector PR repository. Compare that canonical identity with the checked-out repository's `nameWithOwner`; stop and return the mismatch if they differ or if `headRefName` differs from the checked-out branch. Otherwise retain the PR number, title, body, base and head refs, head commit, and repository owner/name for the coordinator.

## Retry policy

For a failed read-only discovery, intake, or status command, retry that exact command automatically at most once and only for an authentication, permission, API, or suspicious sandbox/network failure. Use host/escalated execution for the retry when sandbox or network access is implicated. Do not inspect credentials or run login for the user. If the retry fails, retain the final command and output. This automatic retry does not apply to replies, resolutions, or any other write.

## Reviewer state and requests

At every intake boundary, retain `headRefOid` and read requested reviewers, completed reviews, and top-level pull request comments:

```bash
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{number}/requested_reviewers
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{number}/reviews --paginate
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{number}/comments --paginate
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{headRefOid}
```

Retain every requested reviewer's login and type. For every review, retain the author login and type, `commit_id`, state, body, `submitted_at`, and review ID. Retain each top-level comment's ID, author, body, timestamps, and `minimized` state. Keep non-minimized comments from the documented Bugbot identity `cursor[bot]` and Copilot identity `copilot-pull-request-reviewer[bot]`, plus every exact `Bugbot run` trigger regardless of author. An exact trigger is reviewer-state evidence, not a feedback queue item. Treat other identities as automated only when explicit bot metadata proves it; unknown identities remain human-owned. Retain the current head commit's committer timestamp for Bugbot's timestamp fallback.

Classify Bugbot and Copilot independently against the current `headRefOid`, in this order:

- `Unavailable`: authentication, permissions, configuration, or an API failure prevents that reviewer from being read or requested.
- `In flight`: Copilot appears in requested reviewers, or an exact `Bugbot run` trigger newer than the current head commit is still within the 15-minute active window and has no later Bugbot result.
- `Current`: the latest completed review's `commit_id` equals `headRefOid`.
- `Stale`: the latest completed review's `commit_id` differs from `headRefOid`.
- `Missing`: no completed review or active request exists.

Use reviews with a non-empty `submitted_at` as completed and select the newest `submitted_at` for that reviewer. When a Bugbot result has no review commit, classify a result newer than the current head commit as `Current` and an older result as `Stale`; an exact trigger newer than the head and without a later result is `In flight`. Return the timestamps with the state so the coordinator does not present this fallback as commit-backed coverage.

These states describe review coverage, not whether an individual finding is
actionable. Return findings from completed reviews even when their commit is
`Stale`; the coordinator checks each one against current source. A SHA mismatch
alone does not invalidate a finding or block fixing it.

## Review round budget

Set one GitHub automated-review budget from the local review intensity chosen
for the starting candidate:

- lightweight or direct local review: one round;
- parallel full local review: at most two rounds.

A round is one head-coverage phase for Bugbot and Copilot together, even when
only one reviewer needs a request or one request fails. At initial intake,
usable completed or in-flight Bugbot or Copilot coverage constitutes round one;
if neither exists, the first request phase becomes round one. A missing reviewer
may join that same initial round. Earlier completed reviews reused after
current-source validation also satisfy the initial round rather than forcing a
new one.

The coordinator records rounds used and remaining. The sentinel only reports
reviewer state. Entire findings and reviews never consume this budget.

Do not request another round merely because a push advanced `headRefOid`.
Lightweight and direct changes stop after their initial round. For a parallel
full change, the coordinator may spend the second round after a verified fix is
pushed when the fix materially changed reviewed code or fresh coverage is
otherwise justified. Never request a third round. Once the budget is exhausted,
continue refreshing existing GitHub findings and Entire without treating the
lack of another GitHub request as unsettled work.

Request a `Missing` reviewer when the workflow needs that source. Reuse a
completed `Stale` review unless relevant code changed materially, the finding's
applicability cannot be established from source, or the user requested fresh
current-head coverage. A request must fit the current round or open a permitted
next round. When warranted, start the applicable calls in the same
orchestration phase:

```bash
gh pr comment "{pr-url}" --repo "{owner}/{repo}" --body "Bugbot run"
gh pr edit "{pr-url}" --repo "{owner}/{repo}" --add-reviewer @copilot
```
